Definition: An AI-based machine system that, for a given set of objectives, makes predictions, recommendations, or decisions influencing real or virtual environments
Synonyms: artificial intelligence system, automated decision system
Notes: The ontology uses this project class as a subclass of AIRO AISystem; NIST and the EU AI Act use different source definitions.

Definition: The risk of adverse consequences from decisions based on incorrect or misused models
Source: Federal Reserve SR 11-7 / OCC 2011-12 (2011); ontology ModelRisk
Synonyms: algorithmic risk, AI risk, model governance risk
Notes: AI risk and algorithmic risk are used as alternative labels in the ontology; their scope may differ by source.

Definition: An AI system classified as high-risk under a regulatory framework and subject to enhanced governance requirements.
Source: EU AI Act Art. 6 + Annex III
Notes: The EU AI Act Article 6 includes routes involving Annex I and Annex III, subject to its conditions. The ontology separately represents HighRiskTier; its alternative labels are not necessarily equivalent to this system class.

Definition: A formal policy setting out principles, rules, or standards for developing, deploying, and overseeing AI systems.
Source: ontology/ai-finance-governance.ttl, AIGovernancePolicy; CBA public AI approach page
Notes: The ontology class includes firm and regulatory policies. CBA’s public AI approach and its named internal Group Artificial Intelligence Policy are separate records.

Definition: A structured internal framework or toolkit used to govern AI without necessarily being a separately published formal policy
Source: ANZ and CBA 2024 annual reports; ontology AIGovernanceFramework
Synonyms: responsible AI framework, AI governance toolkit
Notes: Kept distinct from AI governance policy to avoid overclaiming publication status

Definition: A public firm report or web page that contains evidence about AI governance
Source: ANZ and CBA 2024 annual reports; ontology FirmAIGovernanceDisclosure
Notes: A disclosure may describe a policy or practice but is not automatically a policy itself

Definition: The degree to which the outputs and decision logic of an AI system can be understood by human stakeholders
Source: NIST AI RMF section 3.5; EU AI Act Article 13; HSBC 2024 Principles
Notes: The ontology lists these as alternative labels, but their scopes can differ. Right to explanation is an alternative label of ExplainabilityObligation, not Explainability.

Definition: Independent or controlled review, testing, re-validation, and approval of a model before implementation or continued use.
Notes: ModelValidation is a subclass of AIDeploymentApproval. The ontology lists model approval and pre-deployment review as alternatives for the broader approval process, not necessarily equivalent to validation.

Definition: Policies and processes governing AI systems or services provided by external vendors
Synonyms: vendor AI governance, AI outsourcing governance, third-party model governance
Notes: Governance processes concerning external AI providers; the ontology also uses vendor AI risk and related risk labels as alternatives. Their scopes may differ.

Definition: An internal committee or function responsible for oversight and accountability of AI systems
Source: CBA, Goldman Sachs, HSBC and JPMorgan 2024 annual reports; ontology AIGovernanceBody
Synonyms: AI risk committee, model risk committee, AI ethics board
Notes: The ontology models bodies for CBA, Goldman Sachs, HSBC and JPMorgan; CBA’s cited disclosure does not explicitly state an AI oversight remit.

Definition: Systematic and unfair discrimination in AI outputs, typically arising from training data or model design
Source: EU AI Act Art. 10; HSBC 2024 Principles
Synonyms: algorithmic bias, AI fairness risk, unfair discrimination
Notes: The ontology treats bias as a risk; fairness and discrimination are related concepts whose scope can differ.

Definition: Risk from inaccurate output bias privacy intellectual-property security or misuse concerns arising from generative AI
Synonyms: GenAI risk, generative AI operational risk
Notes: NAB calls generative AI an emerging operational-risk area; Goldman describes several specific AI model risks

Definition: A set of principles for developing and deploying AI systems in an ethical, transparent, and accountable manner
Source: CBA public AI approach; NIST AI RMF
Synonyms: ethical AI, trustworthy AI, human-centred AI
Notes: CBA publishes an undated principles-based AI approach; NIST AI RMF provides a structured governance framework; terminology and scope vary across institutions and jurisdictions

Definition: A classification level assigned to an AI system based on its assessed risk
Source: EU AI Act Art. 6; MAS AIRM
Synonyms: AI risk category, risk classification, impact level
Notes: A general ontology class for risk classifications; firm model tiering is not asserted equivalent to EU high-risk classification.

Definition: A process to demonstrate that an AI system meets requirements of an applicable regulatory framework before deployment or market placement.
Notes: The ontology uses a general class; EU AI Act Article 43 sets requirements for specified high-risk systems. Regulatory audit is a contextual alternative, not necessarily an equivalent process.

Definition: The ability of humans to monitor, understand, intervene in, and where necessary override the outputs or decisions of an AI system
Source: EU AI Act Art. 14; NIST AI RMF
Notes: Human-in-the-loop, control, and supervision are ontology alternative labels; mechanisms and scope vary by source.

Definition: Policies and processes ensuring that data used to train and operate AI systems is accurate, complete, representative, and fit for purpose
Notes: Article 10 requires appropriate data-governance and management practices for training validation and testing data sets used by high-risk AI systems

Definition: A scoped source assertion with topic, interpretation, status and linked evidence.
Notes: A source-scoped statement; grouping statements by topic does not establish legal equivalence or implementation.

Definition: A published commitment or scoped provision for challenging AI use or outcomes.
Source: Westpac public AI principles; ASIC RG 271; EU AI Act Article 86
Notes: Represented by the literal topic “Contestability” on governance statements, not a standalone class. Distinguish firm commitments, general complaint procedures, and conditional legal rights.

Definition: Classification of the evidential role of a source statement.
Notes: Free-text description of the evidential role or status of a statement, not an implementation-confidence measure.

Definition: Internal classification of models by complexity, exposure and reliance.
Notes: Mapped to JPMorganTiering2025Statement, a source-specific individual, not to an equivalent class. Its topic is “Risk tiering”; it is not asserted equivalent to EU high-risk classification.

Definition: An internal review and sign-off process a firm must complete before deploying an AI system into production.
Synonyms: AI pre-deployment review, model approval process
Notes: The ontology models ModelValidation as a subclass; validation and approval are not automatically identical.

Definition: A regulatory or policy requirement that AI system outputs and decisions be interpretable and explainable to affected parties.
Synonyms: interpretability obligation, right to explanation, transparency requirement
Notes: A requirement distinct from the Explainability principle; alternative labels and legal rights can differ in scope.

Definition: A formal internal policy governing model risk, including model monitoring, validation, approval, and use controls.
Notes: A model risk policy is not automatically a published AI governance policy.

Definition: A short excerpt, paraphrase, or source-specific note that supports a knowledge graph assertion.
Notes: A snippet can be an exact quotation or another source-specific note; consult its source and status.

Definition: An observed use of a term by a firm, regulator, or standard-setting body, linked to the concept it denotes and the source where it appears.
Notes: An observed usage and its mapping do not by themselves establish equivalence across sources.
